title: What the camera is deciding for you
teaches: The four decisions behind every photograph, what Bird-watching mode picks for you, and what you get back by picking one of them yourself

blocks.text: Point a camera at a heron and press the button, and the camera makes four decisions in the time it takes you to breathe in. It decides how wide to open the hole in the lens, how long to leave the shutter open, how hard to amplify what the sensor caught, and where to [[focus|focus]]. Everything else, from the colour of the light to how much of the scene is sharp, follows from those four.

A scene mode such as Bird-watching is a set of preferences for those decisions: a fast [[shutter|time]], [[focus|focus]] set to keep up with something that moves, and whatever [[ISO|sensor]] that costs. It is a good set of preferences. The trouble with it is not that it chooses badly but that it chooses the same way in a dim wood at dawn as on a bright shore at noon, and it never tells you which decision it had to compromise on.

This first lesson is a tour of the four. Each one has a figure below it that works on a real photograph: move the control and the picture changes the way the camera would really have changed it. Nothing here is a simulation of a *style*; it is the optics and the arithmetic of a [[Nikon Coolpix P950|subject]], the camera this course is written for.[^why-p950]

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Every photograph is four decisions: [[aperture|aperture]], [[shutter|time]], [[ISO|sensor]] and [[focus|focus]].
A scene mode makes all four for you, and tells you nothing about what it gave up.

blocks.text: A lens gathers light from a scene and bends it back to a point. It can only [[focus|focus]] properly on one distance at a time: things at exactly that distance land on the sensor as points, and everything nearer or farther lands as a small disc.[^circle] When the disc is smaller than the sensor can resolve, it passes for a point and we call it sharp. That is all [[depth of field|sharp]] is: the band of distances whose discs are too small to notice.

blocks.caption: A point, the cone of light the lens throws from it, and the disc it lands as
blocks.task: Move the point off the focused distance, then narrow the aperture until it looks sharp again

blocks.text: Narrowing the [[aperture|aperture]] trims the edges off that cone, so the disc shrinks and the sharp band widens. Opening it up does the reverse, which is how a photographer throws a background away. On a camera with a small sensor the sharp band is very wide to begin with, so a soft background takes some work: you want the lens long, the subject close, and the background far behind it.

blocks.caption: A perched bird, with the aperture and the focused distance in your hands
blocks.task: Throw the background out of focus while the bird stays sharp

parts.title: How long the shutter stays open

blocks.text: The [[shutter|time]] decides how long the sensor collects. Everything that moves during that time, in the scene or in your hands, is recorded along its whole path rather than at one instant. Those are two different blurs with two different cures, and telling them apart in your own pictures is one of the most useful things in this course: if the whole frame is smeared, it was you; if the bird is smeared against a sharp branch, it was the bird.

blocks.caption: A bird in flight, with the shutter and the stabiliser in your hands
blocks.task: Find a shutter speed that freezes the bird, then turn the stabiliser off and see which blur comes back

blocks.text: The stabiliser works on your hands and not on the bird, which is why it cannot save a picture of something moving. A tripod is the same bargain. Slow shutters are not only a hazard, though: left open on purpose, they turn moving water into something no eye ever sees.

blocks.caption: A stream, on a tripod, with the shutter open as long as you like

blocks.text: Light arrives as photons, and a sensor pixel does nothing cleverer than count them. A count of ten thousand is steady; a count of fifty is not, because counting is a game of chance and a small count comes out rough.[^shot-noise] [[ISO|sensor]] is the amplifier applied afterwards: it does not add light, it multiplies the count you got, and multiplies its roughness with it. That roughness is what we call grain or noise.

blocks.caption: The photons a mid-grey is counted from, at each ISO, and the grain that leaves
blocks.task: Raise the ISO until the count is visibly rough

blocks.text: Those three dials all do the same job, which is to decide how much light makes the picture, and each one charges a different price: the [[aperture|aperture]] in depth of field, the [[shutter|time]] in movement, the [[ISO|sensor]] in grain. A change of one **stop** on any of them halves or doubles the light, so a stop given up on one can be taken back on another.

blocks.caption: Three dials, one scene, and how far the exposure is from right
blocks.task: Knock the exposure off, then put it back by moving a different dial

blocks.text: The P950's zoom runs from 24 mm to 2000 mm, which is an extraordinary range and the reason to own one.[^equivalent] Zooming in does not bring you closer; it narrows the wedge of the world that lands on the sensor and throws away everything outside it. What is left is magnified, and so is every problem: your shake, the heat shimmer over a field, and the fact that the lens cannot open as wide at the long end.

blocks.caption: The same animal across a field, from 24 mm to 2000 mm
blocks.task: Fill half the frame's height with the animal

blocks.caption: The widest the lens will open, at every zoom
blocks.task: Zoom past 1200 mm and read what the lens has left

blocks.text: This is the bargain at the heart of a superzoom, and it is worth seeing plainly rather than being disappointed by it later: at 2000 mm you are working at f/6.5, which is two and a half stops darker than the wide end, with a shake problem that wants a shutter eight times faster. The camera in Bird-watching mode solves that for you by raising the ISO, quietly.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A stop is half the light or twice it, on any of the three dials.
The long end of the zoom costs light, and magnifies shake along with the bird.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the four decisions

items.question: The whole frame is smeared, background and all. What happened?
options: The camera moved while the shutter was open
The bird moved
The ISO was too high
The aperture was too wide
items.why: When everything smears together, the camera moved. A smeared subject against a sharp background is the other blur, and only a faster shutter fixes that one.

items.question: You narrow the aperture from f/2.8 to f/5.6. What else must change to keep the exposure?
options: Two stops: a longer shutter or a higher ISO
Nothing, the camera is already right
Two stops faster a shutter
The white balance
items.why: f/2.8 to f/4 is a stop, and f/4 to f/5.6 is another, so two stops of light have gone and must come back from the shutter or the ISO.

items.question: What does raising the ISO actually do?
options: Amplifies the light the sensor caught, roughness and all
Makes the sensor more sensitive to light
Lets more light through the lens
Opens the shutter for longer
items.why: The sensor's sensitivity does not change. ISO multiplies the count that was made, so a small, rough count becomes a bright, rough one: that is the grain.

items.question: Why is a soft background hard to get on this camera?
options: The small sensor keeps a very wide band of the scene sharp
The lens is not sharp enough
The zoom does not go long enough
The shutter cannot go slow enough
items.why: A small sensor means a short real focal length, and short lenses hold a wide band in focus. Length, a close subject and a distant background are the way round it.

items.question: At 2000 mm the lens opens no wider than f/6.5. What follows?
options: Less light, so a slower shutter or a higher ISO just when shake is worst
Deeper depth of field, which is always welcome
Nothing, the camera compensates
The picture is sharper
items.why: The long end is darker and shakier at once, which is why pictures at full zoom are so often grainy or soft. Knowing that is half of working around it.

learned: Every photograph is four decisions: aperture, shutter, ISO and focus.
A stop is half the light or twice it, and a stop given up on one dial can be taken back on another.
Camera shake smears the whole frame; a moving subject smears only itself.
Grain is a counting problem, not a flaw in the camera.
The long end of the zoom costs light and magnifies every wobble.

why-p950.title: Why this camera
why-p950.text: The figures run on the Nikon Coolpix P950's real numbers: a 6.17 by 4.55 mm sensor, a 4.3 to 357 mm lens (24 to 2000 mm equivalent) opening to f/2.8 at the wide end and f/6.5 at the long one. Another camera would move the numbers and leave the ideas where they are.

circle.title: Circle of confusion
circle.text: The disc a point lands as is called the **circle of confusion**, and the largest one that still passes for a point is usually taken as the sensor's diagonal divided by 1500: about 0.005 mm here, against 0.029 mm on a full-frame camera.

shot-noise.title: Shot noise
shot-noise.text: A count of N photons is uncertain by about the square root of N, so a count of 10,000 is out by 1% and a count of 100 by 10%. This is **shot noise**, and it is a property of light rather than of cameras: no sensor can avoid it.

equivalent.title: Equivalent millimetres
equivalent.text: A lens's real focal length only says what it will do once you know the sensor size behind it. Makers quote the focal length a 36 by 24 mm camera would need for the same view, so 357 mm on this sensor is quoted as 2000 mm. The crop factor here is 5.6.
